item.title: Pioneering MOF-303 in Lithium–Sulfur Batteries: Coordination Defect Engineering Enables Accelerated Sulfur Redox and Dendrite-Free Plating
item.description:

ACS Energy Letters | 🔬 Research Article
💡 First application of MOF-303 in Li–S batteries, using ball-milling to create coordination defects (ligand defects, oxygen vacancies) in D-MOF-303. This defect engineering yields hierarchical porosity, smaller particles, and enhanced Lewis acidity, enabling strong polysulfide chemisorption, faster redox kinetics, and dendrite-free lithium plating. The modified separator delivers high capacity retention, rate capability, and humidity resilience, advancing practical high-energy Li–S batteries.
🏷 lithium-sulfur battery · MOF-303 · defect engineering · polysulfide shuttle · dendrite-free plating

Advanced Energy Materials | 🔬 Research Article | 🔓 Open Access
💡 This study uniquely links calendering intensity to electrochemical and cost-energy tradeoffs in NMC/LMFP blend cathodes, revealing composition-dependent densification limits absent in NMC alone. It shows moderate calendering preserves rate benefits in 70/30 blends, while hard calendering degrades both blends. Nb-stabilized NMC further improves cyclability and energy retention, offering a practical pathway to optimize microstructure, durability, and cost.

💡 Ni-MOF precursors enable atomic-level control of active Ni²⁺ content and Ni–O covalency in high-entropy O3 cathodes. This balances capacity and stability, unlike conventional oxides with excess or insufficient Ni²⁺. The reinforced covalent network yields reversible phase transitions, thin CEI, fast Na⁺ kinetics, and stable cycling (~130 mAh g⁻¹, 92.6% ICE).

💡 This work pioneers heterogeneous EDL nanostructure engineering via cation-anion coordination, creating ion-transport pathways that stabilize Zn anodes. It achieves record Zn²⁺ transference (0.89), 30,000-cycle full-cell stability, and practical Ah-level pouch cells, offering a new paradigm for durable aqueous zinc-ion batteries.

💡 This review uniquely systematizes built-in electric fields (BIEFs) in rechargeable batteries, covering formation mechanisms, characterization, theoretical calculations, and roles in anodes, cathodes, and electrolytes. It bridges knowledge gaps by linking BIEF engineering strategies to design principles, offering actionable guidance for suppressing instability and enhancing kinetics in next-generation high-energy, long-life batteries.

It thereby unifies disparate battery chemistries and guides future adaptive host design.
